cues.text: Good to have you here.
However you're sitting right now, let that be enough.
No adjusting, no fixing.
Just arrive, exactly as you are.
You can be quiet to yourself.
Let your eyes close, or let them go soft, resting downward.
Nothing to prepare for.
Nothing to get right.
Just you, and a little quiet time.
Breathe in.
Let it out slowly.
One more.
In…
and out.
I want to tell you something you probably already know,
but maybe haven't thought about in a while.
Everyone has a voice inside them.
A voice that talks to you, quietly, all day long, especially when something goes wrong.
Let's think about that voice for a minute.
Imagine, just for a second, you did something small today.
Nothing serious.
Maybe you forgot something.
Maybe you said the wrong thing to someone.
Maybe you made a little mistake at work, or at home.
Now notice, in your mind, how that inner voice usually reacts to something like that.
For a lot of people, that voice gets sharp pretty fast.
That's what we'd call being self-critical.
Self-critical means talking to yourself harshly,
the way you'd never actually talk to someone you cared about.
It sounds like, "Why did I do that?" or "I always mess things up." It's quick to blame.
Slow to forgive.
Notice if that voice feels familiar to you.
No need to judge it, just notice it.
Breathe in.
Now, here's something worth imagining.
Picture a close friend of yours.
Someone you actually love.
Now imagine that same friend comes to you,
and tells you they made that exact same mistake you made earlier today.
What would you actually say to them?
Chances are,
you wouldn't say "you always mess things up." You'd probably say something softer.
Something like, "It's okay, it happens." Or "You're being too hard on yourself.
It’s okay to make mistakes."
That kind,
gentle voice—the one you naturally use with people you love—that’s called being self-compassionate.
Self-compassionate, such a beautiful word.
Being self-compassionate means treating yourself with the same kindness you’d give to a friend:
warmth instead of judgment, understanding instead of blame.
Repeat with me: “I can be self-compassionate.”
Breathe out slowly.
Here's the interesting part.
You already know how to be self-compassionate.
You do it all the time, for other people.
The voice isn't missing.
It's just usually pointed somewhere else, away from yourself.
Let's practice pointing it inward, just for these few minutes.
Think again about that small mistake from earlier.
Or if nothing comes to mind,
think of any small thing about yourself you sometimes judge a little too harshly.
Now, instead of reacting the old way,
try speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to that friend.
Silently, in your mind, try saying something like, "It's okay.
You're allowed to make mistakes." Or simply, "You're doing your best."
Notice how that feels, even if it feels a little unfamiliar,
even a little strange at first.
That's completely normal.
Kindness toward yourself can feel awkward if you're not used to it,
like a muscle that hasn't been used in a while.
Breathe in.
You don't need to believe these words perfectly, right away.
You're just practicing.
Just letting your inner voice soften, a little, right now.
Self-critical thoughts often show up automatically, fast, and loud.
Self-compassionate thoughts usually need a little more effort, at least at first.
They're quieter.
Gentler.
They take a moment to choose.
But every time you choose them, they get a little easier to find.
Breathe out.
Imagine, for a moment, that you’re holding your own hand,
like you would hold the hand of someone you want to comfort.
You don't actually need to hold your hand.
Just imagine the warmth and comfort of that feeling.
Let yourself receive a little of your own kindness right now.
A few words, if you'd like to keep them.
I don't have to be perfect to be worthy of kindness.
I can talk to myself the way I'd talk to someone I love.
Mistakes don't make me any less deserving of care.
I am allowed to be gentle with myself.
I am doing my best, and that is enough.
Take one more slow breath in.
Stay with this feeling a little longer if you'd like.
There's no rush to leave this softness behind.
When you're ready to come back, start noticing small, real things again.
Whatever is supporting your body right now.
Any sound nearby.
Your breath, still slow, still yours.
Move your fingers first, gently.
Then your feet.
Whenever it feels right, let your eyes open.
That kind voice inside you, the one you just practiced listening to, it's always there.
It doesn't disappear when this meditation ends.
It's simply waiting for you to reach for it, especially on the days you need it the most.
